prompt: By this lesson's standard, when is a test case finished?
hint: Think of who runs it, and what they have.

choices.text: When it checks the right requirement
choices.why: Necessary, and not enough: a correct case only its author can run is a note.

choices.text: When a stranger, unable to ask, reaches your verdict with it
choices.why: Right: that is the stranger test.

choices.text: When the team lead has reviewed it and signed it off in the tool
choices.why: A reviewer who knows the application fills gaps a stranger would trip on.

choices.text: When its author has run it once, following the page, and it passed
choices.why: The author knows what every word meant; the run proves the case works for one person.

prompt: Why is a stranger who guesses worse than a stranger who asks?
hint: What does the run log show afterwards?

choices.text: Guessing takes longer than asking
choices.why: It is usually quicker, which is why it happens.

choices.text: A guess always makes the case fail
choices.why: A guess often makes it pass, which is the problem.

choices.text: The case gets a verdict for a different test, and nothing records that
choices.why: Right: their show, their quantity, their idea of a correct price, under your case's id.

choices.text: Strangers may not change the data in a case they were handed
choices.why: There is no such rule; the trouble is that the case left the data open.

prompt: The automation courses turn manual cases into programs. What kind of stranger is a program?
hint: What does it do with a gap in the case?

choices.text: An easy one: it can read the source code to fill gaps
choices.why: A script follows the case it was given; it does not read the application to guess intent.

choices.text: The strictest: it does exactly what the case says and guesses nothing
choices.why: Right: every gap in the case becomes a gap in the program.

choices.text: Not a stranger at all, since its writer knows the application
choices.why: The person who writes the program reads the case, and the case is what has to carry the answers.

choices.text: A lenient one, because it accepts whatever the page shows
choices.why: It accepts only what it was told to check, which is the expected result.

prompt: Match each vague phrase from Ana's draft to what a finished case writes instead.
hint: A value or an observation, never another word.

pairs.right: State: reserved, on the Order page

right_distractors: the right total for that account

prompt: Four rewrites of "check the price is correct". Which one still leaves the stranger asking?
hint: A replacement has to be something found on a screen.

choices.text: The Order page shows R$ 81,00
choices.why: A place and a value: nothing to interpret.

choices.text: The total is the right amount for a member
choices.why: Right: "the right amount" moved the question and kept it.

choices.text: The Order page reads 10% off and R$ 81,00
choices.why: Both values are on the page, as boxoffice writes them.

choices.text: The total in bold on the Order page is R$ 81,00, written with a comma
choices.why: Long, and every part of it can be checked.

prompt: A step says "press the blue Book button at the bottom left of the form". What is wrong with it?
hint: What does the verdict depend on?

choices.text: It fails the day the button moves, while booking still works
choices.why: Right: name a control by its words; the look is not what the case checks.

choices.text: Nothing: more detail always helps a stranger
choices.why: Detail the verdict does not depend on is a reason to fail that is not a defect.

choices.text: Colour words have to be written as hex codes such as #0000ff
choices.why: The colour should not be in the step at all.

choices.text: It should say "submit the form" so it covers any button
choices.why: That is vaguer, and leaves the stranger to find out how.

prompt: An observable expected result names a ___ and a thing that should be there, such as the Order page and the words State: reserved.
hint: Where to look.

prompt: A case expects "Order 1001 reserved." It passes the first time and fails every time after, with boxoffice behaving as R4 says. Why?
hint: What did the second run start from?

choices.text: boxoffice numbers orders at random
choices.why: They count up from 1001 after each restart.

choices.text: Without a restart, the next order is 1002: the state moved
choices.why: Right: state the starting point, or leave the number out of the result.

choices.text: The first run used up the member account
choices.why: An account books as often as it likes; what moved is the order count.

choices.text: A booking for the same show cannot be made twice, so the run ends early
choices.why: The second booking was reserved too, as order 1002.

prompt: After a fresh start Hamlet has 80 seats. TC-BOOK-01, two tickets, is run three times without a restart. How many seats does the Shows page list for Hamlet afterwards?
hint: Each run takes its own seats.

prompt: A case checks the member discount by booking The Seagull, tonight's show. Run after work, it answers "Booking for this show has closed." What is the best fix?
hint: Is the hour what this case checks?

choices.text: Keep it as it is: it passes for whoever runs it in the morning
choices.why: A case whose verdict depends on who runs it, and when, has no verdict.

choices.text: Change the expected result to the closing message
choices.why: Then it fails in the morning, and stops checking the discount at all.

choices.text: Book Hamlet instead, a week away, so the hour cannot matter
choices.why: Right: when time is not what a case checks, its data stays far from the edge.

choices.text: Add a step that waits until the show has started and then books again
choices.why: After the start booking stays closed; waiting only makes the refusal certain.

prompt: A newly created account that was never confirmed books two Hamlet tickets and is charged R$ 160,00 with 0% off. Is that a defect?
hint: R5: who gets the 10%?

choices.text: Yes: every account is a member and should get 10% off
choices.why: R5 calls a confirmed account a member; this one is not confirmed.

choices.text: No: under R5 it is not a member yet
choices.why: Right: which is why a case names the account and its state together.

choices.text: Yes, because the case said "a member" and the result differs
choices.why: The case was vague; the application followed the requirement.

choices.text: It cannot be known without reading the code of discount
choices.why: R5 answers it; no code is needed.

prompt: Which of these are ways the stranger can make a precondition true? Choose all that apply.
hint: The lesson names three.

choices.text: Stop boxoffice and start it again
choices.why: Yes: a reset gives the state lesson 1 describes.

choices.text: Follow set-up steps written in the precondition
choices.why: Yes: "sign up ana@example.org and do not confirm it".

choices.text: Run another case first, named by its id
choices.why: Yes, and it is the most fragile of the three.

choices.text: Ask the writer which state they had
choices.why: The stranger cannot reach the writer; that is the premise.

choices.text: Edit boxoffice.py so the state holds at start-up
choices.why: That tests a different program.

prompt: What does a rewrite of a vague case start with?
hint: Patching keeps the old shape.

choices.text: Replacing each vague word with a value, top to bottom
choices.why: That is patching, and it keeps a title like "Booking works".

choices.text: Deciding the one thing the case checks
choices.why: Right: the title says it, and the rest is built to check that.

choices.text: Running the draft to see what boxoffice does
choices.why: Then the expected result copies the screen.

choices.text: Adding a screenshot of every page the steps visit
choices.why: Pictures do not answer which show or how many tickets.

prompt: TC-BOOK-04 books three tickets for The Little Prince. Why not five?
hint: Which rules of R5 could apply to five?

choices.text: Five is outside R4's range
choices.why: R4 allows 1 to 6.

choices.text: At five the group discount applies too, hiding which rule was checked
choices.why: Right: three leaves the member's 10% as the only discount in play.

choices.text: The Little Prince has too few seats for five
choices.why: It has 200.

choices.text: Three makes the total a round number, which is easier to compare on the screen
choices.why: R$ 81,00 is no rounder than other totals; the reason is which rule applies.

prompt: Put the steps of TC-BOOK-04 in order.
hint: The form, top to bottom, then the result.
items: Type member@example.org in the E-mail field
Choose The Little Prince in the Show list
Type 3 in the field that reads Tickets (1 to 6)
Follow the link Shows at the foot of the page
trap: Pressing Book before choosing the show books whatever the list showed first.

prompt: A confirmed member books 4 tickets for Hamlet, at R$ 80,00 each, Student unticked. What total should the expected result give, in reais?
hint: Below five tickets, one discount.

prompt: Why can no question in this course grade whether a stranger can run your case?
hint: What is the only instrument that measures it?

choices.text: Cases are too long to fit in an answer box
choices.why: Length is not the obstacle.

choices.text: The course has not written those questions yet
choices.why: No question could be written for it, now or later.

choices.text: Only a stranger running it measures it, and a key is fixed before your case exists
choices.why: Right: a key cannot know what your words mean to someone who is not you.

choices.text: Grading it would need the course to see your computer and your browser while you work
choices.why: Even with your screen, the measure is a person who does not know what you meant.

prompt: Your stranger stops at step 3 and asks which show you meant. What do you do?
hint: An answer out loud hides a hole.

choices.text: Answer it briefly, so the run can carry on to the end and its verdict stays fair
choices.why: The verdict is not what this run is for; the question is.

choices.text: Write the question down, and tell them to do what they think the case means
choices.why: Right: the question is a defect in the case, and what they do next shows how they read it.

choices.text: Stop the session: a stranger who asks has failed it
choices.why: The stranger cannot fail; only the case can.

choices.text: Point at the right option without saying anything
choices.why: Pointing is answering.

prompt: After fixing the case from the first stranger's questions, why hand it to a different person?
hint: What does the first one know now?

choices.text: Two verdicts are needed before a case counts as finished by the team
choices.why: It is about questions, not a count of verdicts.

choices.text: The first one would be bored by a second run
choices.why: Boredom is not the issue.

choices.text: The first now knows the answers and cannot find the holes
choices.why: Right: they have stopped being a stranger to this case.

choices.text: A tester should check the fixed case, and the first stranger was not one
choices.why: A non-tester is better: a tester fills gaps from habit.

prompt: Why is the cold read weaker than handing the case to a stranger?
hint: What can the writer not do?

choices.text: You cannot forget what you meant
choices.why: Right: the words clear only to you stay clear.

choices.text: Four days is too long, and the application changes in the meantime
choices.why: boxoffice is the same file; the gap is there so you forget details.

choices.text: A writer is not allowed to run their own case
choices.why: A writer runs it once on purpose, in section 05.

choices.text: It skips restarting boxoffice, so the state is wrong
choices.why: The cold read restarts it too.

prompt: Precondition: the usual test account. Steps: book a few tickets for Hamlet. Expected: the Order page shows the correct discount. Which phrases must be replaced before a stranger can run it? Choose all that apply.
hint: A value or an observation, or the stranger asks.

choices.text: the usual test account
choices.why: Yes: whose usual, and in what state?

choices.text: a few tickets
choices.why: Yes: how many?

choices.text: the correct discount
choices.why: Yes: correct according to what? Write the percentage and the total.

choices.text: Hamlet
choices.why: A show by name: nothing to ask.

choices.text: the Order page
choices.why: A place the stranger can find.

prompt: Your stranger reached the same verdict as you, but booked The Little Prince where you meant Hamlet. Is the case finished?
hint: The verdict is not the only thing compared.

choices.text: Yes: the verdicts agree, and that is the test
choices.why: Agreement here is luck; the case let them run a different test.

choices.text: Yes, as long as both shows give the same discount
choices.why: They do today; the case still does not say which show it checks.

choices.text: No: doing something other than you meant is a defect in the case
choices.why: Right: name the show in the data and the steps, then hand it to someone new.

choices.text: No: the stranger made a mistake and should run it again
choices.why: The stranger followed what was written; the fix goes in the case.
